episode.observableAction: On a Saturday afternoon in the living room of the apartment, the subject sits on the floor with colored pencils and a half-finished drawing of a bus on a sheet of printer paper. Their younger sibling is beside them, pushing a small toy car back and forth. The subject pauses, looks around the room, and then starts checking under a cushion and behind a low table, saying they can’t find the blue pencil they were using. The sibling stops rolling the car and joins the search, peering under the coffee table and lifting the edge of a rug. The subject pulls open a shallow drawer in a TV stand and rustles through loose papers and a remote control, then kneels to look under the couch. The sibling crawls closer to the couch and reaches an arm underneath, then shakes their head and sits back. A caregiver, passing through from the kitchen carrying a mug, notices them on the floor and asks what they’re looking for. The subject holds up the drawing and taps the uncolored part of the bus, saying they need the blue pencil. The caregiver sets the mug on a side table, bends down, and suggests checking the small plastic box where school supplies are usually kept. The subject goes to a low shelf, pulls out a cloudy plastic box with a snapped-on lid, and opens it on the floor. Together, the subject and sibling sift through pens, stubby crayons, and a glue stick. The sibling picks up a green pencil and offers it, but the subject shakes their head and keeps rummaging. The caregiver leans over, lifts a folded worksheet from the box, and reveals a short blue colored pencil underneath. The subject grabs it, says that’s the one, and returns to the drawing spot on the floor. The sibling follows and resumes rolling the toy car nearby while the subject presses the blue pencil to the paper and begins coloring in the bus windows. The caregiver picks up the mug again and walks back toward the kitchen.

episode.observableAction: On a late Saturday morning in the apartment living room, the subject kneels by a low table with a cardboard box of crayons, a sheet of paper showing an unfinished drawing of the family on a city bus, and several crayons scattered on the rug, while the younger sibling sits nearby tapping two toy figures together; when the subject reaches for a dark green crayon and cannot find it, they push aside other crayons in the box, pat the rug, and look under the table, then call out toward the kitchen that the green one is gone. Caregiver 1 walks in drying their hands on a dish towel, asks which color is missing, and joins the search by lifting a couch cushion, sliding the crayon box aside, and checking under a folded blanket on the couch. The sibling crawls closer and peers under the table, then pulls out a red crayon and sets it on the paper before going back to the toy figures. After a moment, the caregiver spots the dark green crayon partly under the edge of the subject’s drawing, taps it with a finger, and pushes it fully into view; the subject picks it up, says they see it now, and leans over the paper to color in the bus seats while the caregiver straightens the blanket on the couch and walks back toward the kitchen and the sibling resumes tapping the toy figures together on the floor.

On a Saturday afternoon at the low table in the apartment living room, the subject sits with a sheet of lined paper and a short list of snack items written in uneven block letters while the younger sibling leans on the table watching; Caregiver 1 stands nearby holding an open wallet and says they have enough money for only one extra treat, then looks at the subject and tells them to help the sibling decide between a small bag of chips and a chocolate bar, pointing to each word on the list in turn. The subject turns to the sibling and slowly reads the two options aloud, tapping the paper with a finger, then asks which one the sibling wants more. The sibling looks back and forth between the subject’s face and the list, says “chocolate,” then pauses and asks if the chips will last longer; the subject answers that the chips have more pieces to share and lightly taps the chips line again. After a few seconds, the sibling nods and says “chips,” and the subject circles the chips item on the paper with a pen. Caregiver 1 nods, tucks a bill into the subject’s hand along with the folded list, and says they will all walk to the store together in a few minutes as the subject sets the pen down and the sibling leans closer to look at the circled word.

episode.observableAction: On a warm early Saturday evening along the commercial street, the subject walks beside Caregiver 1 carrying a folded piece of paper and a small bill, stops with them outside a narrow corner grocery, and listens as Caregiver 1 points to the handwritten list and reminds the subject to get one small bag of the specific chips they circled earlier and a carton of milk, then says they will wait by the bus stop bench a short distance away; the subject nods, pushes open the grocery door, and disappears inside while Caregiver 1 walks to the bench and sits facing the storefront, occasionally glancing toward the entrance until, several minutes later, the subject comes back out holding a plastic bag with a milk carton and a single small chip bag visible through the side, walks over to the bench, and hands the receipt and remaining change to Caregiver 1 as they both turn to head back toward the bus stop sign.

On a cloudy Sunday afternoon at the low table in the apartment living room, the subject sits with a supermarket flyer, a scrap of lined paper, and a pen while the younger sibling leans on the opposite side of the table and Caregiver 1 stands nearby holding an open wallet; Caregiver 1 says they can afford only one special outing snack for the next day and asks the subject to help the sibling choose between a box of frozen ice cream bars and a family-size bag of chips pictured on the flyer, pointing to each photo in turn, then sets the wallet on the table and steps back. The subject reads the labels under both pictures aloud, taps the ice cream box image and mentions that it has fewer pieces, then taps the chips picture and notes that it has more pieces to share on the bus ride home, while the sibling looks back and forth between the two pictures and asks if the ice cream will melt before they get back. The subject points to the chips again and says those can stay in a backpack without a cooler, the sibling hesitates, then says they want the chips for the outing, and the subject writes “big chips bag” on the scrap paper and circles it. Caregiver 1 picks up the wallet, glances at the circled words, nods, and says they will buy that one when they go to the store later, as the subject sets the pen down and slides the flyer toward the sibling, who traces a finger around the chips picture.

episode.observableAction: On a quiet Sunday afternoon in the apartment living room, the subject sits at the low table with a school notice and a bus schedule printout while the younger sibling leans on the back of the couch and Caregiver 1 stands nearby drying their hands on a dish towel; Caregiver 1 reads the notice about an optional after-school art club that meets twice a week and costs a small monthly fee, points to the line about needing bus fare on meeting days, and explains that if they pay for the club and extra bus rides there will not be money for the usual weekend snack chips for a while, then asks the subject and sibling to think about whether to sign up; the subject looks from the notice to the bus schedule, the sibling asks if that means no big chips bag on outings, and Caregiver 1 nods and says they can still do regular groceries but not the extra snack, then places the notice on the table in front of the subject and says they need an answer by tomorrow morning as the sibling shifts on the couch and the subject folds the top edge of the paper and sets it beside the bus schedule.

On a cool Saturday early afternoon in the apartment living room, the subject sits at the low table with the after-school art club notice unfolded beside a bus schedule and a blank permission form while the younger sibling lies on the couch flipping through a TV guide and Caregiver 1 stands near the doorway drying a plate with a dish towel; the subject clears their throat and says they have decided not to join the art club so the family can keep buying the big chips bag for weekend outings, then slides the unsigned permission form toward Caregiver 1, who walks over, picks it up, and asks if they are sure; the subject nods and taps the bus schedule, mentioning the extra fares, and the sibling looks over from the couch and says they are glad the chips are staying, swinging their feet against the cushion; Caregiver 1 folds the blank form, sets it on top of the notice, and says they will tell the school there is no sign-up on Monday, then places the papers on a shelf by the hallway as the subject stacks the bus schedule with other leaflets on the table and the sibling returns to studying the TV listings.
